title: “Proof” is running on Broadway though July 19th! #broadway #ayoedebir...
transcript: I've been praying for Ayo Edebiri to come to Broadway for years, so this revival of the Pulitzer winning play Proof, also starring Don Cheadle, Kara Young, and Jin Ha, was one of my most anticipated shows of the season. From an acting standpoint, it didn't disappoint. Edebiri plays the daughter of a famous mathematician who loses his sanity, and there's some question of to what extent she takes after her father. In this role, Edebiri is able to flex her intense dramatic chops alongside the wry comedy and quirky energy she's often known for. Don Cheadle also gave a really lovely performance with an infectious blend of warmth and fiery passion that made you totally understand why she idolized him. And my beloved Tony winner Kara Young is playing against type here, but also excellent. And the interplay between her and Edebiri are some of the strongest scenes in this production. This was surprisingly my first exposure to this play, which was incredibly successful when it first premiered, and I found it pretty engaging on a surface level, but I left surprisingly unmoved by. And I've been really struggling to put my finger on why. So much so that I did something I usually don't do. I read several reviews before writing my own, and from what I gather, this production, directed by Tommy Kail, goes for a more grounded feel that strips away some of the mystery that once gave it a riveting sense of intrigue. But that didn't totally explain it for me, because there's also a very emotional core to this play beyond the titillating (or not so titillating) sense of mystery: This protagonist, who cared for her father so deeply, and now is wrestling not only with her grief, but with this double edged inheritance. And I wonder if, in an attempt to move away from this narrative of, like, casting doubt on this protagonist, maybe Kail was trying to spotlight that emotional family dynamic instead, which is maybe why it came through so beautifully in the lead performances. But then trying to make that the central throughline of the production put the direction at odds with this script. Not because there isn't plenty of depth and pathos to mine from the script, but because it's not written to fuel the action of the play. Catherine feels more or less the same about her father at the beginning of the play as she does at the end. And without that tension, we don't get a catharsis.
